say.text: That is not the right choice.
The chart feels like the burn's own job, so it pulls the eye first. It sits in the secondary survey, which comes after the primary survey has checked the airway.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check the order: the primary survey, airway first, comes before any burn-specific work.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Talking now feels safe, but swelling builds over the next hours and fluids add to it. A calm voice today does not guarantee the airway later.
Ask which threat could end this patient in minutes, and which task can wait a few minutes of the workup.
A burn patient is on the trolley: soot on the lips, voice hoarse, talking in full sentences. The nurse already has the fluid chart open.
Which reasoning puts the airway first?

choices.label: Airway can close within hours; the fluid plan can wait minutes
The burn-specific chart is the real first priority
A talking patient has a safe airway, so the check can wait
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The primary survey checks the airway first, because it can close within hours. The burn chart is secondary and waits its turn.
That is not the right choice.
Stridor is a late sign. By the time it shows, the swelling is already narrowing the airway, so waiting for it means waiting too long.
That is not the right choice.
A patient who speaks well today can still lose the airway as swelling grows. Speech tells you about this minute, not the next several hours.
Think about how this airway will look in six hours, and what fluid does to swollen tissue.
A 40% scald patient is talking normally, with no stridor. Fluids have just started, and the swelling round the face is growing.
Why should you secure the airway now, rather than watch it?

choices.label: Swelling grows over hours with fluid, so a tube is easier now
Stridor is the signal, so a patient without it can wait
Full sentences prove the airway is protected for now
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Oedema builds over hours and resuscitation adds fluid, so the window for an easy tube closes. Act while the window is open.
That is not the right choice.
A chest film feels like the first and safest test. It is often normal early, so a clear film cannot settle the airway question.
That is not the right choice.
A blood gas samples oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood. It feels like it should reveal lung injury, but it measures gas exchange, not the airway lining.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Ask what the test sees: the inside of the tube, not the chest picture or the blood.

say.text: Ask which test looks at the airway itself, rather than at the lungs or the blood.
A man was found in a barn fire. He has soot on his lips and a hoarse voice. His chest film at arrival is clear.
Which test would settle whether the airway lining has been hurt?

choices.label: Fibreoptic bronchoscopy, looking straight at the airway
Repeat the chest X-ray in six hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Bronchoscopy looks directly at the airway and shows soot, swelling or redness below the cords, which is what confirms the injury.
That is not the right choice.
Dissolved oxygen is a small amount. It does not make up for blood that cannot carry oxygen, so the reading stays falsely normal in this poisoning.
That is not the right choice.
A normal number feels reassuring, but it measures what the probe sees. In carbon monoxide poisoning that number is falsely normal.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A confident normal number is how carbon monoxide gets missed. Ask which gas the reading can see.

say.text: Think about what the device's light can separate in the blood, and what it cannot.
A woman is found after a gas heater leaks in a closed room. She has a headache, and her oximeter reads 100%.
Why does this normal reading fail to rule out carbon monoxide?

choices.label: It counts oxygen-bound haemoglobin alone, so carbon monoxide hides
Her blood holds dissolved oxygen, so carrying capacity is still normal
A normal saturation proves oxygen is reaching her tissues
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Carboxyhaemoglobin is a separate share that the oximeter cannot tell apart from oxyhaemoglobin, so a measured level is needed.

A straight scale feels tidy, but pain does not climb in step with depth. A partly injured nerve supply can hurt less than an intact one.
That is not the right choice.
Nerves are not gone in every deep burn. Reduced pain points to partial nerve injury, and full thickness is the dry, painless, leathery burn.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Reduced pain is one clue among several, not the grading scale.

say.text: Think about what nerve endings do when they are only partly damaged, rather than on a scale from mild to severe.
A forearm burn hurts less than the skin around it, and it refills slowly when you press.
Why does lower pain not, on its own, make this the deepest burn?

choices.label: Pain needs surviving nerve endings, so partial damage can hurt less
Pain tracks depth in a line, so less pain means deeper
Less pain means nerves are gone, so it is full thickness
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Deep partial injury leaves some nerve endings working, so pain falls without the burn becoming full thickness.
That is not the right choice.
Arms look like large areas, so they seem to deserve a leg figure. Each arm carries the smaller adult value on the chart.
That is not the right choice.
The back of the trunk is one of the big regions. Counting it as a small figure drops almost half the area, so check each region against the chart.
An adult has burns over the whole back of the trunk and both arms. The front of the body is untouched.
Using the adult rule of nines, what is the total body surface area burnt?
Yes. The posterior trunk is 18%, and each arm is 9%, so 18 plus 9 plus 9 gives 36%.

The whole 24-hour total is not run in the first window. Only half of it goes into the first 8 hours, so divide half, not the whole.
That is not the right choice.
Halving is right, but the half here is spread over 24 hours. The first half belongs to the first 8 hours, so the window is shorter.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Halving the total and dividing by the window are two separate steps. Check each one.

say.text: A 90 kg adult has a 30% burn. You are using the Parkland key of 4 mL per kilogram per percent, and the first window runs from the time of burn.
What is the hourly rate for the first 8 hours?
Yes. Total 4 x 90 x 30 is 10,800 mL. Half is 5,400 mL, and over 8 hours that is 675 mL/h.
That is not the right choice.
Output looks like fluid loss, so more output seems to call for more fluid. But high output means the kidneys are well perfused, and extra fluid risks swelling.
That is not the right choice.
The formula is a sum of weight and burn size. It cannot know about depth, delay or inhalation, so output tells you whether the sum fits this patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A formula gives a starting rate, and the patient's output is the check on it.

say.text: A 60 kg adult is on the formula rate. At six hours, urine is 60 mL/h, and blood pressure is steady.
Why should the rate change, rather than stay on the formula?

choices.label: Hourly output is the live check on whether the starting estimate fits
High output means fluid is leaving, so more fluid should replace it
The formula is exact, so output only records the result

say.text: Yes. The formula is a starting estimate. Hourly output above the 30 to 50 mL/h adult band means the rate is more than needed, so reduce and recheck.
That is not the right choice.
Silver sulfadiazine is the broad, painless cream most wards reach for, so it feels like the match. Its known problem is leucopenia, not black staining or low sodium.
That is not the right choice.
Mafenide penetrates eschar and suits the ear, so it feels like the stronger choice. Its signature problem is acidosis, which this picture does not describe.
A silver-treated burn dressing has turned black, and the serum sodium is low.
Which topical agent fits this picture?
Yes. Silver nitrate stains black and can cause hyponatraemia, so the sodium needs watching with its dressings.
That is not the right choice.
Half a mL per kilogram is the adult figure. A child's kidneys and higher metabolic load call for a larger figure per kilogram.
That is not the right choice.
A fixed adult band ignores body weight. A child's target is worked per kilogram, so the figure must scale to this child.
A 14 kg three-year-old has a 20% scald and is on crystalloid.
What hourly urine output is the target?

choices.label: 14 mL/h, about 1 mL per kilogram per hour
7 mL/h, half a mL per kilogram per hour

say.text: Yes. Children aim at 1 mL per kilogram per hour, so 14 kg gives 14 mL/h. That is the end of the quiz.
Airway first, size the burn honestly, start with the formula, then let the urine decide.

cards.q: Which comes first in a burn patient with soot and a hoarse voice?
cards.a: The airway, in the primary survey, because it can close within hours.
Fibreoptic bronchoscopy. A clear chest film often misses it early.

cards.q: Why is a painless, dry, white burn full thickness?
cards.a: Nerve endings are destroyed, and the skin is dry, leathery and does not blanch.

cards.q: Adult rule of nines: posterior trunk and each arm?
How much of the Parkland total goes in the first 8 hours?
cards.a: Half of the 24-hour total, run over 8 hours from the time of burn.

cards.q: What urine output target do adults and children aim for?
cards.a: Adult 0.5 mL/kg/h (30 to 50 mL/h); child 1 mL/kg/h, with the rate titrated to it.

cards.q: Which topical agent stains black and can lower sodium?
cards.a: Silver nitrate; mafenide is the one that causes acidosis.
